title: How to Make UGC Videos Brands Pay For (2026): Formats, Hooks, Scripts
excerpt: The 6 UGC formats brands buy, 10 hook templates, a 30-second script, phone filming setup and delivery specs, for UGC creators in the US and Canada.
content:
How to Make UGC Videos Brands Pay For (2026)

Brands do not pay UGC creators for their audience. They pay for footage they can run: a 20-second clip that stops the scroll on a Meta or TikTok ad, a product demo for an Amazon listing, a testimonial for a landing page. That changes how you should film. This guide covers the formats brands buy, hook and script templates, phone filming setup, delivery specs, and how to tell which of your videos actually work.

It is written for creators in the US and Canada pitching US and Canadian brands, but the craft is the same anywhere. If you are still deciding whether UGC is for you, start with UGC vs influencer marketing.

Show Brands You Can Do This

Every format below makes a strong portfolio clip. Put your best three on a free UGC portfolio brands can open from one link.

Build My Free UGC Portfolio

Table of Contents

1. The 6 UGC formats brands buy
2. Hooks: the first 3 seconds
3. A 30-second UGC script
4. Filming UGC on a phone
5. Storytelling without sounding like an ad
6. Using TikTok trends in UGC
7. Delivering files brands can use
8. How to know which videos work
9. Mistakes that get UGC rejected
10. FAQ

1. The 6 UGC Formats Brands Buy

Most UGC briefs ask for one of six formats. Knowing the name of each one makes briefs faster to read and your portfolio easier to scan.

FormatWhat it looks likeWhere brands use it
Talking-head testimonialYou, to camera, explaining why you switched to the productMeta and TikTok ads, landing pages
Problem / solutionShow the annoying problem, then the product fixing itCold traffic ads (people who do not know the brand)
Unboxing / first impressionPackaging, texture, first use, honest reactionLaunches, gifting campaigns, organic posts
Routine / day in the lifeThe product inside a real morning, workout or cleaning routineLifestyle and skincare brands, Reels
Demo / before and afterClose-up proof: the stain gone, the skin texture, the gadget workingAmazon listings, product pages, retargeting ads
Listicle / 3 reasons"3 reasons I keep rebuying this" with quick cutsAds that need a clear message in 15 seconds

If you are building your first portfolio, film one problem/solution, one talking-head testimonial and one demo. Those three cover most briefs you will see. For product ideas you already own, use the 50 UGC product ideas list.

2. Hooks: The First 3 Seconds

On paid social, most viewers decide in the first second or two. Brands judge UGC by its hook more than anything else, and many will ask for several hook versions of the same video. Use these templates and swap in the product:

  1. "I did not expect a $[price] [product] to [result]."
  2. "Stop scrolling if you [have problem]."
  3. "3 things I wish I knew before buying [category]."
  4. "This is the [product] everyone on my feed keeps asking about."
  5. "I have tried [number] [category] and this is the only one I rebought."
  6. "POV: you finally found a [product] that [result]."
  7. Start with the result on screen (the clean counter, the finished look), then rewind.
  8. "If you [specific situation], you need to see this."
  9. A quick honest objection: "I thought this was overhyped. Here is what happened."
  10. Show the product in an unexpected place or use, then explain.

Film every video with three different hooks on the same body. It takes ten extra minutes and is the easiest way to look like a professional: the brand gets three ads to test instead of one.

3. A 30-Second UGC Script Structure

SecondsBeatExample (vitamin C serum)
0-3Hook"I did not expect a $24 serum to fix my dull winter skin."
3-8Problem"Every winter my skin looks grey by noon, and makeup sits on top of it."
8-20Product + demoClose-up of the dropper and texture, two drops pressed in, morning light on skin.
20-26Proof"Two weeks in, I skip foundation on most days." Side-by-side in the same light.
26-30Call to action"It is linked here if your skin gets like this too."

Write the script as you would say it to a friend, then cut every sentence that does not move the viewer to the next beat. Never invent results: say what actually happened in your own words. US brands also need claims that hold up under FTC endorsement rules, so avoid medical or guaranteed-result claims unless the brief gives you approved wording.

4. Filming UGC on a Phone

  • Frame 9:16 vertical, 1080p or 4K, 30fps. Keep important text and the product away from the bottom fifth of the frame, where captions and buttons sit on TikTok and Reels.
  • Light: face a window in daylight. Turn off overhead bulbs that mix colors.
  • Audio: a quiet room with soft furnishings beats any editing trick. A clip-on lavalier mic is the first gear worth buying.
  • B-roll list for every product: packaging, texture or close detail, product in hand, product in use, the result, and a clean shot of the label.
  • Clean background: real but tidy. Brands want a believable home, not a studio, and not visible competitor products.
  • No watermarks and no on-screen platform UI. Export from your editor, not from a downloaded TikTok.

Do Not Let Gear Stop You

Most UGC that runs as ads is filmed on a phone. What brands reject is shaky framing, poor audio and a weak hook, not the absence of a camera. Fix those three first.

5. Storytelling Without Sounding Like an Ad

Good UGC feels like a friend's recommendation. A simple story structure keeps it from sounding like a commercial:

  • Start where the viewer is. Their problem, in their words, not the brand's tagline.
  • One moment, not a feature list. The first time the product made a difference is more convincing than five benefits.
  • Show, then say. Let the demo carry the claim, and keep the voice-over short.
  • Keep one honest detail. "The smell is strong at first" makes everything else you say more believable.
  • End on a next step. A light call to action the brand can keep or cut.

6. Using TikTok Trends in UGC

Trends can make UGC feel native, but there is a catch: most trending sounds are licensed for personal posts only, not for ads. If the brand will run your video as a paid ad, use the trend's format (the caption style, the transition, the joke structure) and either no music, royalty-free music, or tracks from the platform's commercial music library. Ask the brand which one they want before you edit.

For organic posts on your own account, trends are useful practice: they show you which hooks and formats earn watch time before you pitch them to a brand.

7. Delivering Files Brands Can Use

  • Deliver an edited version with captions and a clean version without captions or music, so their editor can add their own.
  • Send the hook variations as separate files.
  • Name files clearly: brand_product_hook1_v1.mp4.
  • Share one folder link with view and download access, and check it in a private browser window before sending.
  • Agree on revisions up front (one round is standard for starter packages).
  • Only include raw footage if the agreement says so. Raw clips are worth more, so price them as an add-on. See UGC rates and add-ons.

8. How to Know Which Videos Work

Brands judge paid UGC on ad numbers. You will not always get them, but asking shows you think like a marketer, and the answers make your next pitch stronger.

MetricWhat it tells youHow to ask
Hook rate (3-second views / impressions)Whether your first 3 seconds stop the scroll"Which hook had the best 3-second view rate?"
Hold rate (watch time)Whether the body keeps attention"Where did viewers drop off?"
Click-through rateWhether the video makes people curious enough to click"Did one version get more clicks?"
Cost per purchaseThe number the brand cares about most"Did any version beat your current ads?"

For your own organic test posts, use the analytics in TikTok and Instagram: average watch time and the retention graph show exactly where your hook or story loses people. Our guide to TikTok analytics for brand deals shows which screens to screenshot for your portfolio.

Turn good results into proof: one line in your portfolio such as "Hook 2 became the brand's best-performing ad for March" is worth more than any follower count. Brands that see results also come back, which is how one-off gigs become monthly retainers.

9. Mistakes That Get UGC Rejected

  • A slow start: logo, greeting or "Hey guys" before the hook.
  • Reading the brief word for word so it sounds scripted.
  • Claims the brand cannot legally run ("cures acne", "lose 10 pounds").
  • Trending audio baked into a file meant for ads.
  • Messy background with other brands' products in shot.
  • Missing the deadline without a message. Brands rebook creators who communicate.

Turn Your Best Clips Into a Portfolio

Brands hiring UGC creators open portfolios, not camera rolls. Publish your best three clips with rates in a few minutes.

FAQ

How long should a UGC video be?

15 to 30 seconds for most paid social ads, filmed vertical (9:16). Film a little longer than the brief asks so the brand can trim, and always deliver the hook as a separate clip they can swap.

Do I need a lot of followers to make UGC?

No. Brands buy UGC for their own ads and pages, so they judge your samples, not your audience. A portfolio of 6 to 8 clean clips matters more than follower count.

Can I use trending TikTok sounds in UGC?

Not in anything the brand will run as an ad. Most trending sounds are licensed for personal use only. Use the trend's structure or caption format instead, and use royalty-free or the platform's commercial music library when music is needed.

What equipment do I need to start making UGC?

A recent phone, window light and a quiet room are enough to start. A $20 to $40 lavalier mic is the first upgrade worth buying, because brands reject bad audio faster than average video.

Should I deliver raw footage?

Only when it is in the agreement. Raw clips let the brand re-edit and make more ads from your work, so most creators either include them in a higher package or charge for them as an add-on.
